subject: Business
title: Co-Founder Dynamics
description: A micro-lesson that makes Co-Founder Dynamics usable.

hook.text: Jobs and Wozniak built Apple. Then Jobs forced Wozniak out. Co-founder splits are brutal.

buildup.text: About 65% of startups fail due to co-founder conflict, per Harvard Business School.

discovery.text: The best pairings combine complementary skills: one builds, one sells, one strategizes.

twist.text: Friends make risky co-founders if they can't have hard conversations about money and control.

climax.text: Y Combinator recommends a co-founder prenup — a written agreement on roles, equity, and exits.

punchline.text: Choose a co-founder like a marriage. The divorce costs the same.

quiz.question: What percentage of startups fail due to co-founder conflict?

details.summary: Co-founder dynamics determine startup success as much as the business idea itself. The relationship between co-founders affects every decision, and disagreements about vision, equity, roles, and workload are the leading cause of early-stage startup failure before product-market fit.
details.whyItMatters: Co-founder conflict is cited as the number one reason startups fail at the earliest stages, ahead of running out of money or building the wrong product. Getting the founding relationship right is the most important pre-launch decision.
takeaways: Co-founder conflict is the leading cause of early-stage startup failure
Clear role definition, equity agreements, and vesting protect all parties
Complementary skills and shared values matter more than friendship alone

faq.question: How should co-founders split equity fairly?
faq.answer: Equal splits sound fair but ignore differing contributions. Consider who contributed the idea, who has more relevant experience, who is investing more time, and who brings critical skills. Use vesting schedules so equity is earned over time.

faq.question: What is a vesting schedule and why is it essential for co-founders?
faq.answer: Vesting means equity is earned over time, typically four years with a one-year cliff. If a co-founder leaves after three months, they forfeit unvested shares. Without vesting, a departing co-founder keeps full equity for minimal contribution, devastating the remaining team's motivation.
